Dada. An anti-art, anarchist movement born during World War I, roughly from nineteen sixteen to nineteen twenty four, that rejected reason, logic, and aesthetic convention in a spirit of absurdist rebellion. Emerging simultaneously in neutral cities like Zurich, Berlin, and New York, Dadaists weaponized nonsense, chance, and readymades against what they saw as the rationalist folly that had plunged the world into carnage.

The movement was founded at the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich in nineteen sixteen by exiles fleeing the war. Hugo Ball, Tristan Tzara, and Emmy Hennings performed sound poetry and absurdist theater that challenged every assumption about what art could be. Marcel Duchamp's Fountain from nineteen seventeen, a porcelain urinal signed R. Mutt, epitomizes the Dada stance perfectly. The artwork is the gesture, the provocation itself, not the object's aesthetic merit.

Dadaists worked with chance operations, collage, photomontage, nonsense poetry, and readymades. Hannah Höch pioneered photomontage. They deliberately embraced accident and ugliness over craft. Cabaret performances featured simultaneous poetry and sound, and periodicals like Dada 3 and Der Dada spread the movement's manifestos across Europe and beyond.

The movement had distinct regional branches. Berlin's version was political and photomontage-heavy. New York Dada featured Duchamp and Man Ray. Paris Dada was literary and proto-Surrealist. This decentralized, international character meant Dada had no unified aesthetic or style. Its only real coherence was rebellion, making it more a spirit of cultural rejection than a formalized movement. More than anything else, it rejected the notion that art should have consistency or coherence at all.
